title: Inside the Perimenopause Industrial Complex
gist: After the FDA removed black-box warnings on hormone therapy last fall, four leading perimenopause telehealth startups — Midi, Winona, Alloy, and Evernow — saw a 490 percent surge in web traffic from 2023 to 2026, creating estradiol patch and progesterone shortages and pulling venture-funded virtual clinics toward growth-at-all-costs platform strategies aimed at a market of 43 million US women aged 35 to 54.

insights.claim: The FDA's removal of black-box warnings on hormone therapy last fall was the regulatory trigger that converted a long-suppressed treatment category into a demand surge.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A single label change reopened a multi-decade-suppressed prescribing category — watch for the same mechanic in other post-2002-scare drug classes.
insights.quote: We’re challenging outdated thinking and recommitting to evidence-based medicine.
insights.locator: Last fall, the US Food and Drug Administration removed

insights.claim: A SimilarWeb analysis commissioned for this article found that Midi, Winona, Alloy, and Evernow together saw a 490 percent uptick in web traffic from 2023 to 2026, which SimilarWeb characterized as an organic demand surge rather than paid-acquisition inflation.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A near-5x traffic move labeled organic is the strongest available public proxy for private-company revenue growth in this segment — a valuation input ahead of any funding round or IPO.
insights.quote: there has been an “organic demand surge.”
insights.locator: According to an analysis conducted by SimilarWeb

insights.claim: Hormone therapy prescribing collapsed after a 2002 study that led women to overestimate cancer risk, meaning today's boom is a reversal of a two-decade prescribing depression rather than net-new demand.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: The addressable pool includes a large backlog of untreated patients, so early growth rates will overstate the steady-state run rate once the backlog clears.
insights.quote: Hormone therapy had been out of favor for years, after a 2002 study led women who might have otherwise asked for the treatment to overestimate potential cancer risks
insights.locator: Around the time Schrenk was having

insights.claim: The founder of the telehealth company Evernow, Alicia Jackson, joined the Trump administration as director of HHS's ARPA-H less than a month before appearing at the FDA press conference announcing the black-box removal.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: An industry founder placed inside the agency that lifted the category's key restriction is a governance signal worth tracking for further regulatory tailwinds — and for reversal risk if the appointment changes.
insights.locator: Shortly after, the director of the department’s

insights.claim: More than 43 million US women aged 35 to 54 define the addressable market for perimenopause hormone therapy, and virtual clinics are actively jockeying for dominance of it.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A 43-million-person, chronic, multi-year-duration prescription market with no incumbent explains why venture capital has crowded in this fast.
insights.quote: More than 43 million women between the ages of 35 and 54 live in the United States—an enormous market.
insights.locator: Perimenopause typically begins when people

insights.claim: Midi is described as the first menopause unicorn, with competitors Alloy and Evernow also funded and larger telemedicine firm Hers entering the perimenopause category.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A category-leading unicorn plus a public-market telehealth entrant means the pure-plays face immediate distribution competition from platforms with existing subscriber bases.
insights.locator: Some are flush with venture capital funding

insights.claim: Turnkey telehealth services let almost anyone launch a virtual hormone clinic within days, collapsing barriers to entry in the category.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Near-zero entry cost caps long-run margins and makes clinical quality and brand the only defensible moats — commodity price competition is the base case.
insights.quote: thanks to “turnkey” services that help new virtual clinics get started, almost anyone can start selling hormones online within days.
insights.locator: And thanks to “turnkey” services

insights.claim: Midi is one of the few online hormone providers accepting health insurance — and does not work with Medicare or Medicaid — while many rivals are strictly out-of-pocket with subscriptions of up to $200 a month.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Insurance acceptance is Midi's differentiating acquisition channel but caps pricing; the $200/month cash competitors carry higher ARPU with far more churn risk in a downturn.
insights.locator: Midi is one of the few online hormone therapy providers

insights.claim: Midi's CEO shrugged off the question of how the company reaches profitability, explicitly modeling the business on growth-first industry disruptors like Uber.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A named unicorn with no articulated path to profit in a low-barrier category is a late-cycle funding risk — capital availability, not demand, is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: Like industry-disruptor startups before it—Uber, for example—it’s focused on growth, with a goal of becoming a one-stop shop for at least half the population’s health needs.
insights.locator: And make no mistake: This is an effort to eclipse

insights.claim: Midi's stated strategy is to become a national specialized primary care company for women spanning their twenties through fifties, mirroring how Hims and Hers expanded from a single men's health product into a general platform.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: The endgame is a subscription primary-care platform, not a hormone vendor — valuation depends on cross-sell attach rates, so watch GLP-1, supplement, and skincare mix.
insights.quote: We're building out a national specialized primary care company for women
insights.locator: A lofty goal, but one that Midi

insights.claim: Midi's clinicians already prescribe GLP-1s — described as the golden goose of the telehealth world — alongside hormone therapy, plus supplements and a recently expanded prescription skin care line.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Hormone therapy functions as a low-cost acquisition wedge into higher-margin GLP-1 and cash-pay ancillary revenue — the real unit economics live in the attach, not the estrogen.
insights.locator: In addition to HRT, Midi’s clinicians prescribe GLP-1s

themes.theme: Supply shortage as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Estradiol patches have been hard to find since the FDA removed the black-box warning, though the agency has not officially declared them in shortage, and progesterone supplies tightened this June in response to the same surge.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Unlabeled shortages mean demand is outrunning supply without triggering the FDA mechanisms that would let compounders legally fill the gap at scale — a bottleneck on every provider's revenue.
insights.quote: Estrogen patches have been hard to find since the FDA removed the black-box warning label, though they haven’t been officially labeled “in shortage” by the agency.
insights.locator: The popularity of hormone treatments

insights.claim: Suppliers had no incentive to expand capacity because most of these hormone medications are off-patent and not big moneymakers, so the demand shock hit a structurally unresponsive supply base.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Off-patent economics mean shortages persist longer than in branded markets — the pricing power sits with whoever adds generic manufacturing capacity first, not with the prescribers.
insights.quote: Suppliers were not prepared, nor were they especially incentivized to meet demand; most of these medications are off-patent and not big moneymakers.
insights.locator: The popularity of hormone treatments

insights.claim: Because new hormone therapy patients are far younger than the typical menopausal patient, they stay on the medications for much longer, compounding the supply squeeze structurally rather than temporarily.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Longer treatment duration raises lifetime value per patient for providers and permanently raises baseline demand for the underlying generics — a durable volume story, not a spike.
insights.quote: That means they stay on them for a much longer time, further exacerbating supply issues.
insights.locator: New patients who take the medications

insights.claim: More than 50 percent of Midi customers are prescribed some form of hormone therapy, and a recent company survey found nearly 4,000 women had trouble filling a prescription at least once.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Fulfillment failure at this scale is a churn driver the growth metrics do not capture — a virtual clinic that cannot deliver the drug loses the subscription.
insights.quote: We don’t think they understand the extent of the problem
insights.locator: What she’d actually been doing was taking a conference call

insights.claim: No lab test can establish whether someone is perimenopausal because unpredictable hormone variation is the condition's hallmark, so clinicians diagnose almost entirely on self-reported feeling.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: An unfalsifiable diagnosis with a cash-pay treatment is the structural setup for indication creep — and the exact profile regulators eventually revisit.
insights.quote: No lab test can reveal whether someone is or isn’t reaching this life stage, because unpredictable hormone variation is its hallmark.
insights.locator: One might be forgiven for wondering

insights.claim: Midi's stated position is that menopause has more than 100 possible symptoms, a list running from night sweats and low libido to body odor, sensitive teeth, asthma, and dry skin.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: A 100-plus symptom list is effectively a universal qualification criterion — it maximizes funnel conversion and simultaneously maximizes future regulatory and advertising-standards exposure.
insights.locator: The potential customer base is vast

insights.claim: The director of the Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health and medical director of the Menopause Society says the perimenopause hype machine has gotten completely out of hand in pushing hormone therapy for longevity and vague ailments like fatigue.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: The category's most credentialed voices are on record against the marketing thesis — a ready-made source of authority for any future FTC, advertising, or payer pushback.
insights.quote: We are running into a danger zone attributing all these symptoms to perimenopause
insights.locator: Stephanie Faubion, director of the Mayo Clinic’s

insights.claim: A Yale gynecologist who evangelizes for treatment awareness still argues that for most women's stress and low mood, the cause is probably not their hormonal milieu.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Even the category's advocates concede most converted customers are outside the clinical indication — a fragile basis for recurring revenue if sentiment turns.
insights.quote: But is it attributable to their hormonal milieu? Probably not
insights.locator: The way Minkin sees it, life stressors

insights.claim: Midi's leadership argues hormones should be prescribed protectively before symptoms appear, citing unfelt effects like rising blood pressure and cholesterol, worsening insulin sensitivity, and accelerated bone loss.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Reframing hormones as preventive rather than symptomatic expands the funnel from symptomatic women to all aging women — the single biggest TAM lever in the category.
insights.quote: When your hormones deplete, your blood pressure goes up, your cholesterol goes up, insulin sensitivity worsens, and you accelerate bone loss.
insights.locator: OK. Health and wellness, then

themes.theme: Marketing, trust arbitrage, and advertising risk

insights.claim: Midi's claim that 91 percent of patients find relief within two months drew scrutiny from BBB National Programs' National Advertising Division, and the company dropped the claim before action was taken.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Advertising-standards friction is already live for the category leader — a template for how efficacy claims across the sector get walked back.
insights.locator: One of its claims—that 91 percent of patients

insights.claim: Midi's CEO says the acquisition strategy deliberately exploits patients' distrust of traditional medicine, routing through Instagram influencers women already believe in.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Customer acquisition built on institutional distrust is cheap now but hostage to platform algorithm changes and influencer-disclosure rules — a concentration risk in the CAC line.
insights.quote: They feel like doctors have dismissed them and their symptoms, and so they are more likely to trust an influencer that they follow online that they believe in than the traditional health care system.
insights.locator: Midi’s approach to finding new customers

insights.claim: Consumer acceptance of compounded medications was built by cheap off-brand GLP-1s, which normalized both virtual clinics and non-name-brand formulations for a population that would previously have rejected them.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: The GLP-1 boom built the distribution rails and consumer trust that every subsequent cash-pay telehealth category now rides — expect the same playbook applied to the next drug class.
insights.quote: The public has also warmed up to compounded products sold by virtual clinics, because off-brand GLP-1s are so much cheaper than name brands like Ozempic.
insights.locator: Beyond the FDA’s recent removal

insights.claim: Perimenopause content is being consumed as an identity marker, with creators framing it the way late-in-life autism and ADHD diagnoses are framed for women.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Identity-driven adoption is far stickier than symptom-driven adoption, which supports retention but makes the category vulnerable to a backlash cycle like other diagnosis trends.
insights.locator: While I was reporting this story

themes.theme: Clinical quality bifurcation and incentive risk

insights.claim: Telehealth law is lax enough that some hormone sellers prescribe asynchronously off a questionnaire with no visit at all — what Midi's chief medical officer calls vending-machine prescriptions — while Midi requires video visits and mandatory continuing education for its 550-plus clinicians.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: The market is bifurcating into protocol-driven and questionnaire-driven models; a single adverse-event scandal at the low end would trigger rules that raise costs for everyone.
insights.quote: “Vending-machine prescriptions,” Midi’s Jordan calls these operations.
insights.locator: Laws governing telehealth are lax enough

insights.claim: An ARPA-H director who founded a company in this space warns that industry incentives reward chasing the highest profit margins and that the companies doing so are more likely to win.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: When a sitting federal health official says the sector's incentives select for bad actors, expect that framing to precede enforcement or rulemaking.
insights.quote: The incentives are set up to drive people to want to do that, and those companies are more likely to win
insights.locator: Even Jackson, from her perch within RFK Jr.’s department

insights.claim: Midi's former chief medical innovation officer says venture-funded telehealth startups are pressured to return investment tenfold and calls the resulting slope slippery, having left to run a concierge practice that refuses to sell supplements or lotions.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Senior clinical departures citing VC return pressure are a leading indicator of quality drift at growth-stage healthcare companies.
insights.quote: Those companies are pressured to return that investment tenfold
insights.locator: And Heather Hirsch, Midi’s former chief medical

insights.claim: The Mayo Clinic's women's health director flatly calls estrogen face cream garbage for lack of supporting data, while such creams cost about $150 out of pocket for a three-month supply and competitors like Winona sell estrogen-containing skin care as a wrinkle treatment.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: High-margin unproven ancillaries are where the sector's regulatory and reputational risk concentrates — and where a meaningful share of cash-pay revenue sits.
insights.quote: We don't have enough data to support estrogen face cream use. We just don’t.
insights.locator: Some virtual clinics also sell an array of supplements

insights.claim: A prominent ob-gyn critic argues that selling women inadequately studied products under the banner of closing health care gaps is predatory and misogynistic, singling out supplements, face creams, and compounded GLP-1s.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: An organized, credentialed critic base gives journalists and regulators a standing narrative that can crystallize into consumer-protection action.
insights.quote: I will always maintain that selling women inadequately studied products under the guise of closing the gaps in health care and using misleading language is predatory and misogynistic
insights.locator: Jen Gunter, a prominent ob-gyn

insights.claim: Hormone therapy risks are real though historically overstated, with side effects including vaginal bleeding, breast tenderness, and bloating, and contraindications for people with histories of breast cancer, blood clots, or liver disease.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Contraindication screening is the operational weak point of questionnaire-based prescribing — the most likely source of a headline adverse event.
insights.locator: While the risks were overstated for many years

themes.theme: The broader shift to preference-driven medicine

insights.claim: The perimenopause telehealth boom is one instance of a broader swing toward commercialized, preference-driven health care, running in parallel with the explosion of peptides, at-home blood tests, and MRI startups for those who can afford it.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Treat these as one thematic basket driven by the same consumer distrust and cash-pay willingness, not as separate niches — they will re-rate and de-rate together.
insights.quote: all part of a swing toward an ever more commercialized, preference-driven version of health care for those who can afford it.
insights.locator: These conversations are happening all across the country

insights.claim: The growing cohort of women taking hormones constitutes an ongoing treatment group that is more experimental than its members likely realize, since expanded early and preventive use lacks the evidence base of established menopausal indications.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: An outcome study or adverse-event cluster in the younger preventive cohort is the single largest tail risk to the sector's growth trajectory.
insights.quote: Every day, as the number of women taking hormones rises, they join an ongoing treatment group that is more experimental than perhaps they know.
insights.locator: In a few short years, hormone therapy

insights.claim: Hormone therapy has become an unusual point of political convergence, endorsed across medical professionals, liberal feminists, and the Make America Healthy Again movement, even as the same hormones used for trans patients remain vilified by the right.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Rare bipartisan cover lowers near-term political risk for the category, but the coalition is unstable because it rests on contradictory positions about the same molecules.
insights.quote: It’s a weird, politically charged time for hormone therapy.
insights.locator: It’s a weird, politically charged time

insights.claim: Patient demand is being generated peer-to-peer and offline as well as online — the article's central patient discovered hormone therapy from hiking companions after three physicians refused her, and encountered unprompted advocacy again on a later hike.
insights.speaker: Kate Knibbs
insights.so_what: Word-of-mouth conversion at this intensity implies low paid-acquisition dependence in early cohorts, flattering CAC metrics that may not hold as the backlog clears.
insights.quote: A woman in the group started advocating for HRT
insights.locator: She’s still hiking her way through Virginia
